implementation_notes: Mockito's stubbing API is the Java realization of the Test Stub: when(warehouse.hasInventory("Talisker", 50)).thenReturn(false) programmes the canned answer, thenThrow covers the error path, thenReturn(a, b, c) answers consecutive calls, and unstubbed methods return type defaults (null, 0, false, empty collection), as the Javadoc documents. The generated proxy replaces the hand-written stub class Meszaros shows for Java; where the object under configuration is a spy, doReturn(...).when(spy) must be used instead of when(spy.method()), because the latter executes the real method while stubbing. For void methods and for re-stubbing the same method mid-test the doReturn/doThrow/doNothing family is the documented alternative to when().
pitfalls: when(...) is evaluated eagerly, so calling a real method inside it (spies, void methods) executes that method while stubbing; use doReturn/doThrow there.

Unstubbed calls return null, 0, false or an empty collection, so a forgotten thenReturn produces a NullPointerException far from the test's intent or a silently passing path; strict stubs (Strictness.STRICT_STUBS) surface both.
Final classes and static methods cannot be stubbed by the default subclass mock maker; wrap them behind an interface you own instead of enabling the inline agent by reflex.

variants.name: Hand-written stub class implementing the collaborator interface
variants.idiom_name: class implementing the collaborator interface with fixed returns
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Java form, and the one Meszaros documents: an ordinary class implements the collaborator interface and returns the canned value (or throws the canned exception) from the methods the SUT calls. It needs no framework, is checked by the compiler with @Override, and works with final classes, custom class loaders and older toolchains where a proxy mock maker cannot. Prefer it when the double is small, when the team does not want a mocking dependency in the test classpath, or when the stub must carry a little real behaviour; default methods on the interface keep the class from breaking when the interface grows.
pitfalls: Forgetting @Override lets a signature drift silently: the method becomes an overload and the SUT keeps calling the real (or abstract) member.
An interface that keeps growing forces every hand-written stub to be edited; keep consumer-side interfaces narrow or add default methods.
A stub with mutable state shared across test methods creates order dependence; instantiate it per test or reset it in @BeforeEach.
